commentary.bottom_line: Two small simulated studies tested user training, and in one of them physicians who had completed 20 hours of AI-literacy training still lost 14.0 points of diagnostic accuracy when given flawed LLM advice. The other study measured only self-perceived literacy gains, so evidence that training reduces over-reliance on AI is very uncertain, although several studies show the hazard exists.

perspectives.view: Two studies test training, both in simulated settings with small samples. In a randomized trial of 44 physicians in Pakistan who completed 20 hours of AI-literacy training, accuracy fell from 84.9% to 73.3% with flawed LLM advice. A pre-post study of 139 Taiwanese students measured only self-perceived literacy. Certainty is very low because of indirectness, imprecision, and inconsistent findings.

Incorrect AI raised radiologist false negatives to 20.7-33.0% and false positives to 80.5-86.0%. Radiography students changed their answers more often than qualified staff (32.7% vs 19.3%). Trained physicians in the Pakistan trial still lost 14.0 points with flawed advice. This result suggests that training alone may not stop AI errors from reaching patients.

Among 170 US primary care providers, 36.5% felt confident about sources of AI bias, which suggests a knowledge gap exists. The tested program ran 20 hours. No study measured retention, reliance behavior in live use, or delivery fidelity. Staff at 15 Australian hospitals voiced concern about junior staff over-reliance, but the study did not quantify it.

Neither test enrolled clinicians serving Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, and neither measured patient outcomes. The HEAAL framework calls for education that reaches disadvantaged patient subgroups. No study examined whether training changes how AI errors affect those groups.

One endorsing commentary ties institutional training to the assessment of physician liability. A CHAI framework requires training materials to state that AI supports the clinician's care plan rather than overriding it. These sources rest on consensus rather than trial data. Documented training may therefore serve accountability purposes while its effect on reliance remains untested.

The one trained physician cohort received 20 hours of instruction, a staffing cost that would scale with every user a health system trains. No study shows that this investment prevents accuracy loss from flawed AI output. Leaders who adopt training may need to measure its effect locally rather than assume a benefit.

commentary.research_gap: No study has randomized clinicians to training versus no training in a real deployment and measured reliance behavior, error interception, or patient outcomes. Trials that compare training formats and durations, test retention over time, and pair training with workflow safeguards would show whether any form of instruction reduces automation bias in practice.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study that tested training included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; they enrolled physicians in Pakistan and medical students in Taiwan and reported no patient-level data. The evidence therefore cannot show whether training protects patients in settings where language barriers, time pressure, or thin staffing may increase reliance on AI output.
